p: Of all the inventions of mankind, speech is the most important and the least visible. It leaves no ashes, no stones, no bones. The first word ever spoken died on the air the instant it was uttered, and so did the next several billion. When I tell you that the origin of language is the most obscure problem in all the study of man, you will understand why. We are trying to recover the history of something that, by its very nature, left no trace until writing came along to catch it, and writing is no more than five thousand years old.

The difficulty has driven learned men to despair, and sometimes to folly. In eighteen sixty-six, only nine years ago, the Linguistic Society of Paris resolved that it would accept no more papers on the origin of language, so numerous and so fanciful had they become. I have some sympathy with the Society. There had been one theory that language began in imitation of animal cries, which its critics called the bow-wow theory; another that it began in cries of pain and pleasure, called the pooh-pooh theory; and another that every substance rings with its own natural note, like a bell, called the ding-dong theory. These names were given, mostly in mockery, by Professor Max Müller of Oxford, a learned German who is, I believe, still dining in college as I write.
Since my time, the Encyclopaedia tells me, the question has been reopened with better instruments. The evidence now comes from several directions at once, none of them conclusive by itself.

First, there is the body. Human speech depends upon a particular arrangement of the throat, tongue and breath that is unlike that of the apes. Some scholars have tried to discover from fossil skulls and from a small bone in the throat called the hyoid when our ancestors acquired the equipment for speech. The hyoid of a Neanderthal found in a cave in Israel, at a place called Kebara, is said to be very like our own, which suggests, though it does not prove, that the Neanderthals could speak.

Second, there is the inheritance in the cells, which the men of the future can read. They have found a particular element of it, which they name with the letters F O X P two, that is necessary for the fine control of speech; persons in whom it is damaged have great difficulty in speaking. Our own version of it is shared with the Neanderthals. Again, this suggests but does not prove.

Third, there is the evidence of behaviour. A creature that buries its dead with care, or makes ornaments of shell, or paints images upon a cave wall, is very likely a creature that talks, for these are things that carry meanings, and meanings want words. This brings us to a second great question, which the Encyclopaedia calls behavioural modernity.
## When did we begin to behave as we do?

Our species is very old, perhaps three hundred thousand years. But the signs of behaviour that we should recognise as fully human, by which the learned mean art, ornament, long-distance trade, elaborate burial, complex tools of many parts, and the rapid change of fashion from one region and age to another, appear in abundance much later. For a long time the experts held that a sudden revolution of the mind occurred around fifty thousand years ago, perhaps from some fortunate change in the brain, and that after it the human imagination was let loose upon the world. They spoke of a great leap forward.

More recent discoveries have made this view less popular. In Africa, objects of a modern character have been found from much earlier times: at Blombos Cave in South Africa, pieces of red ochre engraved with criss-cross patterns about seventy-five thousand years old, and beads of shell that were pierced to be strung, and, older still, a kind of paint-making workshop of about one hundred thousand years ago, with shells used as pots for mixing ochre. In Morocco, shell beads more than eighty thousand years old. The present opinion, so far as I can make out, is that the modern mind was assembled gradually in Africa over a very long time, with advances and retreats, and that what looks like a revolution in Europe around forty or fifty thousand years ago was largely the arrival there of people who had been modern for a long while already.

I cannot tell you when the first true sentence was spoken. Neither can anyone else. But I can tell you what it meant. A creature without language can show another where food is; a creature with language can tell another where food was last year, where it may be next year, and what the old woman who died last winter said about it. Language allows the dead to teach the living. It allows a band of people to plan, to bargain, to promise and to deceive, all of which, alas, are inseparable. It allows a people to tell stories about where they came from and what they owe to one another. Every law, every religion and every science is made of language.

Above all, language allowed mankind to speak of things that are not present: the absent, the future, the imaginary, the divine. It is in that capacity, I think, that we first came to see ourselves as unlike the beasts. The beasts know the world as it is; we know it also as it might be, and as we fear or hope it will become. It is a magnificent gift and a heavy burden, and it is the beginning of history in the true sense.
